phrases.text: Another quarter hour has compiled successfully. Unlike your project.
Your compiler sends its regards. Mostly warnings.
Time flies. Your build system prefers walking.
Somewhere, a semicolon is ruining someone's afternoon.
You have seventeen tabs open and absolutely no answers.
The bug has been promoted to a feature. Congratulations.
Your CPU believes in you. Your RAM has concerns.
It's a lovely day to delete a cache and pretend it helped.
The code works. Please do not touch anything.
Have you tried turning your expectations off and on again?
One does not simply fix the final warning.
Your TODO list has requested its own TODO list.
The documentation is accurate in a parallel universe.
Another hour, another mysterious dependency.
A clean build is a beautiful and suspicious thing.
Your terminal has seen things it cannot unsee.
Today's forecast: scattered exceptions with a chance of rollback.
You can close one browser tab. As a treat.
The debugger is not judging you. Probably.
Your future self has filed a complaint about this shortcut.
Git remembers. Git always remembers.
Somewhere in this repository is a function named final_final.
The tests are green. Suspiciously green.
Your laptop fan is composing experimental jazz.
Have you considered writing fewer configuration files? Neither have we.
You've been at this for three hours. The outdoors would like a word.
Your chair has enjoyed enough of your company.
The sky is still available without a subscription.
Go and inspect a tree. No debugger required.
Your eyes have requested a maintenance window.
A short walk may resolve dependencies in your brain.
The grass has not been updated, but it's still worth touching.
Water: the original productivity plugin.
Stretch. Even your stack has limits.
You are permitted to leave the computer unattended. It will cope.
Your coffee is not a substitute for daylight.
This is your friendly reminder that knees have a purpose.
Step away from the screen. The pixels will remain loyal.
Fresh air has excellent backwards compatibility.
Your keyboard suggests a brief separation.
Good morning. The bugs have been awake for hours.
Rise and shine. Or rise and negotiate.
Breakfast is not an optional dependency.
The day is young. Your inbox is ancient.
Coffee has entered the chat.
It's almost lunchtime. Even the clock looks hungry.
The afternoon has arrived with no useful release notes.
Another productive morning of moving windows around.
Your calendar says meeting. Your soul says absolutely not.
The sun is doing its best. Consider joining it.
The evening shift is now being supervised by a clock.
Another day of heroic progress and questionable decisions.
It's getting late. Your future self would appreciate sleep.
The moon has checked in. Have you checked out?
Midnight: when every idea sounds like a startup.
Your pillow has opened a support ticket.
This is the hour when variable names become poetry.
The night is quiet. Except for your cooling fan.
Your code can wait until morning. The bugs aren't going anywhere.
Tomorrow is another chance to rename everything.
A watched progress bar never admits defeat.
Beware the wisdom of clocks: they are always counting on something.
A wise programmer knows when to stop. A legendary one has a timer.
Time is money, but this clock accepts neither.
The universe is expanding. So is your downloads folder.
Do not argue with a clock. It has all the time in the world.
If life gives you lemons, check the package checksum.
Your destiny is being processed. Please do not refresh.
An empty inbox is a myth told to junior developers.
The secret to happiness is somewhere under Settings, Advanced.
Every great invention began with someone avoiding another task.
There are two kinds of people: those who back up, and future cautionary tales.
A wise person asks questions. A foolish person clicks Update All.
The clock knows what you did last summer. It was probably debugging.
Somewhere, an ancient server is still running perfectly. Nobody knows why.
Attention. Your mouse has been elected project manager.
This announcement was approved by the International Council of Minutes.
The clock has decided to pursue a career in interpretive dance.
Please remain calm. An unusually punctual second is approaching.
The next minute is brought to you by the previous minute.
I have counted every second. Some of them were deeply disappointing.
Your desk has requested a performance review.
The hour hand and minute hand are no longer speaking.
I was going to tell you a time-travel joke, but you didn't like it.
A small committee of clocks has voted to postpone Tuesday.
The seconds are unionising. Expect delays.
You have unlocked the legendary achievement: Still Sitting There.
I regret to inform you that tomorrow has not been cancelled.
The concept of punctuality is currently in beta.
The clock would like to thank you for your continued existence.
You've been staring at that screen long enough to become a wallpaper.
Another fifteen minutes of pretending this is the final fix.
Your productivity graph has been replaced by a shrug.
This is a clock, not a life coach. Yet here we are.
You have permission to stop optimizing things nobody will notice.
Perhaps the bug is not in the code. Perhaps the bug is destiny.
Your brilliant plan appears to involve more coffee.
Have you tried explaining the problem to a rubber duck with management experience?
One more refactor and the project may become self-aware.
It is now time to consider whether you actually needed another feature.
